name: Colloidal Silver cosmetics

lead: Colloidal silver is a suspension of silver particles, usually 1 to 100 nanometres in size, that appears in some skin products and wound dressings. In skin care it is valued for antimicrobial action, which proponents link to calmer, clearer-looking skin and cleaner wound healing.

Silver nanoparticles are used in bandages, patches and skin grafts for burns and wounds. A few registered trials compare silver dressings for burn and surgical-scar outcomes, including cosmetic scar appearance.

paras: In cosmetics it is used as a topical ingredient or a colourant; in healthcare it is built into dressings applied to wounds. Supplements taken by mouth are a separate use.
Silver can deposit in skin and organs, causing argyria, a blue-grey discolouration that does not go away. Silver dressings can also cause transient discolouration that fades within days.

angle.text: Marketers and wound-care products use silver for its antimicrobial properties on skin. Registered trials compare silver dressings for burn and scar healing.

lead: Colloidal silver products contain silver particles in suspension, and silver nanoparticles have been reported in cosmetic colourants and pigments [1]. In skin care they are used for antimicrobial action, and silver is built into bandages, patches and skin grafts for burns and wounds [1].

The appearance angle is skin and scar quality: antimicrobial dressings aim to reduce infection so wounds heal with a better cosmetic result, and trials register cosmetic scar appearance as an outcome [2][3].
Argyria, a permanent bluish-grey skin change from silver deposition, is the best-known risk [4].

paras: Silver nanoparticles feature in cosmetic colourants and pigments, with acknowledged knowledge gaps about their safety [1]. In medicine they are used in bandages, patches and grafts because of antimicrobial effects [1].

Registered trials include a 2025 pediatric trial comparing chitosan and silver dressings for burn wound and scar healing in 40 children, and a completed 660-patient study of cesarean wound outcomes that lists cosmetic scar appearance among its measures [2][3]. A further trial tested a skin wipe for infection prophylaxis before orthopaedic surgery [5]. These trials concern wound dressings rather than cosmetic creams; results are not summarised here.

Ingesting or chronically exposing the skin to silver can cause argyria, a blue-grey discolouration, most visible in sun-exposed areas, that persists because silver cannot be removed from tissue [4]. Silver dressings can cause transient discolouration fading within 2 to 14 days [1]. Researchers disagree on whether toxicity comes from silver ions, the particles themselves, or both [1].

timeline.event: M. C. Lea records a citrate-stabilised silver colloid [1].
Colloidal silver as an internal medicine is displaced by antibiotics [4].
